passage_text: Researchers at the University of Midwest conducted a controlled laboratory study to investigate how varying amounts of sleep affect cognitive performance in healthy adults. A total of 60 participants (30 males, 30 females, aged 20–35) were randomly assigned to one of three sleep conditions: 4 hours, 6 hours, or 8 hours of sleep per night for three consecutive nights. After the final night, participants completed a battery of cognitive tasks, including a simple reaction time test and a word list recall task. The researchers recorded reaction times (milliseconds) and memory scores (number of words correctly recalled out of 20). Table 1 summarizes the mean values for each sleep condition. The study aimed to determine whether sleep deprivation leads to measurable declines in processing speed and memory retention, and whether the relationship is linear across the sleep duration spectrum. Findings could inform guidelines for shift workers, students, and clinicians managing sleep disorders.
table_data:
Sleep Hours | Mean Reaction Time (ms) | Mean Memory Score (out of 20)
4 | 350 | 12
6 | 320 | 15
8 | 300 | 18
stem: According to Table 1, what is the mean reaction time for participants who slept 4 hours?
explanation: Table 1 lists the mean reaction time for the 4‑hour sleep condition as 350 ms.
trap: Reading the 6-hour or 8-hour row (320 or 300 ms) instead of the 4-hour row.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the design of this study?

options.A: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three sleep durations, so sleep duration was the independent variable.
options.B: Each participant completed all three sleep conditions.
options.C: Participants chose their own sleep duration.
options.D: Only the 4-hour group completed the cognitive tests.

explanation: Correct: A) The passage states random assignment to 4, 6 or 8 hours, so sleep duration is the manipulated variable. Why the others are wrong: B) Each participant was assigned to one condition. C) Durations were assigned, not chosen. D) Table 1 reports results for all three groups.
trap: Choosing B because every participant took the cognitive tests, when each participant was assigned to only one sleep condition.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1 and the passage?

options.A: Mean reaction time was shorter with each increase in sleep duration.
options.B: Mean memory score rose by 3 words from 4 to 6 hours and by 3 words from 6 to 8 hours.
options.C: The reaction-time gain from 4 to 6 hours (30 ms) was larger than from 6 to 8 hours (20 ms).
options.D: Sleep restriction lasting longer than three nights would produce even larger deficits.

explanation: Correct: D) Only three nights were studied, so longer restriction was not tested. Why the others are wrong: A) 350, 320, 300 ms decrease with more sleep. B) 12, 15, 18 differ by 3 each time. C) 350-320 = 30 ms and 320-300 = 20 ms.
trap: Extrapolating the trend beyond the conditions the study actually tested.

stem: According to Table 1, how did the 6-hour group compare with the 8-hour group?

options.A: Reaction time 20 ms slower and memory score 3 words lower
options.B: Reaction time 20 ms slower and memory score 3 words higher
options.C: Reaction time 20 ms faster and memory score 3 words lower
options.D: Reaction time the same and memory score 3 words lower

explanation: Correct: A) 320 vs 300 ms is 20 ms slower and 15 vs 18 words is 3 lower. Why the others are wrong: B) Memory was lower, not higher. C) Reaction time was slower, not faster. D) Reaction times differ (320 vs 300 ms).
trap: Mixing up the direction of the two outcomes, since a larger reaction time means worse performance but a larger score means better.
